title: RGB LED: Mixing Colors with PWM
summary: Synthesize millions of colors using Pulse Width Modulation and additive optical color physics.

steps.title: Expressive Monsters: Crafting Living Light
steps.markdownContent:
Robots need emotion and visual expression! By combining three primary wavelengths of light—Red, Green, and Blue—at varying intensities, we can create any color in the visible rainbow, from energetic yellow to menacing purple or calm cyan.

Because the Arduino Uno does not have true analog output voltage DACs on its digital headers, we use high-speed silicon pulsing—**Pulse Width Modulation (PWM)**—to fool the human eye into perceiving smooth brightness gradients!

```
Timer Register OCR1A ➔ High-Speed 490Hz Pulse Train ➔ Duty Cycle Average ➔ Eye Cone Cells ➔ Perceived Color
```

steps.title: Prior Knowledge Check: Diodes & Voltage Outputs

questions.question: How does a Light Emitting Diode (LED) generate illumination?
options: Forward electric current excites electrons across a semiconductor bandgap, releasing photons
A tungsten filament burns inside an inert vacuum bulb
questions.explanation: LEDs produce electroluminescence when electrons cross a forward-biased semiconductor junction.

questions.question: Why must every color channel of an RGB LED have its own series resistor?
options: Because each color die has a different forward voltage drop and requires dedicated current limiting
To increase the speed of light emission
questions.explanation: Red (~2.0V), Green (~3.2V), and Blue (~3.2V) have different forward voltages and each need independent current limiters.

questions.question: Can the Arduino Uno output true variable DC voltages (like 2.5V) on standard digital pins?
options: No, Uno digital pins only switch between 0V and 5V; they use high-speed PWM pulsing to simulate intermediate levels
Yes, every pin has an on-chip digital-to-analog converter (DAC)
Yes, but only when running on battery power
questions.explanation: The Uno lacks analog DAC outputs on digital headers; it uses Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) to simulate intermediate voltages.

steps.markdownContent:
Before mixing optical light beams and configuring PWM timer registers, let's test your baseline understanding of semiconductor diodes and voltage driving.

Answer the 3 self-check questions below to calibrate your knowledge!

steps.title: Core Concept & Vocabulary: Common Cathode vs Common Anode
steps.markdownContent:
An RGB LED packages three independent semiconductor dies (Red, Green, Blue) into a single 5mm plastic lens with 4 leads sharing a single common pin.

### The Two Packaging Standards:
- **Common Cathode (CC)**: The shared longest lead is connected to **Ground (0V)**. Logic is **Active-HIGH** (`analogWrite(pin, 255)` produces 100% brightness).
- **Common Anode (CA)**: The shared longest lead is connected to **+5V (VCC)**. Logic is **Active-LOW** (sinks current; `analogWrite(pin, 0)` produces 100% brightness, requiring `255 - value` in code).

Toggle between Common Cathode and Common Anode in the schematic below to explore current paths and software logic inversion!

steps.title: How It Works: High-Speed 490Hz PWM Pulse Trains
steps.markdownContent:
Human retina cone cells cannot resolve individual light flashes cycling faster than ~60 Hz due to persistence of vision.

### Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) Physics:
1. ATmega328P hardware timers oscillate output pins at ~490 Hz (or 980 Hz), giving a cycle period of $T \approx 2.04\text{ ms}$.
2. When you execute `analogWrite(pin, 127)`, the timer holds the pin at 5V for 50% of the period, and 0V for the other 50% (**50% Duty Cycle**).
3. The human eye integrates this high-speed photon flux, perceiving a steady 50% brightness!
4. Effective average voltage: $V_{average} = 5.0\text{V} \times \frac{\text{value}}{255}$.

Use the interactive oscilloscope below to inspect pulse waveforms, high-time vs low-time durations, and perceived LED photon flux!

steps.title: Hardware Mission: 4-Pin RGB LED Leadout & Breadboard Wiring
steps.markdownContent:
Examine your 4-pin 5mm Common Cathode RGB LED and breadboard (`comp_breadboard`):

### Lead Identification Tour:
Hold the LED with the flat edge on the plastic rim collar facing right:
1. **Lead 1 (Outer Left)**: Red Anode (Forward drop $V_f \approx 2.0\text{V}$)
2. **Lead 2 (Longest Pin)**: Common Cathode (Connects directly to Uno **GND**)
3. **Lead 3**: Green Anode (Forward drop $V_f \approx 3.2\text{V}$)
4. **Lead 4 (Outer Right)**: Blue Anode (Forward drop $V_f \approx 3.2\text{V}$)

### Resistor Wiring:
Never share a single resistor on the common pin! Connect a separate 220Ω or 330Ω resistor to Lead 1 (Red), Lead 3 (Green), and Lead 4 (Blue). Because red, green, and blue dies have different forward voltage drops, sharing one resistor causes brightness dipping whenever multiple colors illuminate.

steps.title: Coding Basics: Identifying Hardware PWM Pins & Timers
steps.markdownContent:
Can you call `analogWrite()` on any Uno pin? **No!** Only pins wired to internal hardware timer compare registers support PWM.

### Finding the PWM Tilde (~):
Look at the silkscreen on your Arduino Uno next to digital header pins: only pins marked with a tilde `~` (Pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) support PWM:
- **Pins 5 & 6**: Controlled by **Timer0** at **980 Hz** (shared with `millis()` and `delay()`).
- **Pins 9 & 10**: Controlled by **Timer1** (16-bit) at **490 Hz**.
- **Pins 3 & 11**: Controlled by **Timer2** (8-bit) at **490 Hz**.

⚠️ **The Non-PWM Trap**: If you call `analogWrite(8, 128)` on non-PWM Pin 8, it only performs binary threshold switching (>=128 is HIGH, <128 is LOW)!

Test and identify all Uno PWM pins in the interactive checker below!

steps.markdownContent:
Time to blend optical wavelengths! In additive color physics:

- **Red + Green = Yellow**
- **Green + Blue = Cyan**
- **Red + Blue = Magenta**
- **Red + Green + Blue = White**

steps.title: Real-World Robotics: Quadcopter Navigation Beacons & RGB Mood Lighting
steps.markdownContent:
RGB optical mixing and PWM are used extensively in modern robotics:

- **Quadcopter Flight Navigation**: Drones mount high-intensity RGB LEDs under motor arms: solid green for GPS lock, flashing yellow for return-to-home, and pulsing red for low battery.
- **Autonomous Delivery Rovers**: Ground rovers project animated light halos on pavements to signal pedestrians whether they are yielding or turning.
- **Smart Speaker Rings**: Ambient home assistants use 16-channel RGB PWM shift registers to create fluid rotation and pulsing voice feedback animations.

steps.title: Troubleshooting Challenge: Reversed Common Anode & Non-PWM Pin Traps
steps.markdownContent:
Solve the two most common RGB LED hardware bugs:

### Trap 1: Colors Are Inverted (e.g. Red command shows Cyan)
- **Diagnosis**: You have a Common Anode LED instead of Common Cathode! The shared pin is wired to GND or expecting active-HIGH driving.
- **Fix**: Wire the common pin to +5V, and invert firmware values: `analogWrite(pin, 255 - value);`.

### Trap 2: One Color Only Snaps ON or OFF Without Dimming
- **Diagnosis**: That color channel is connected to a non-PWM pin (such as Pin 7, 8, 12, or 13)!
- **Fix**: Move the jumper wire to a PWM pin marked with a tilde `~` (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, or 11).

steps.title: Workshop Safety & Independent Resistor Protection
steps.markdownContent:
Keep your components protected with these electrical rules:

1. **Never Omit Current Limiting Resistors**: Each of the 3 internal LED dies requires its own 220Ω–330Ω resistor to prevent thermal runaway.
2. **Separate Resistors Prevent Brightness Droop**: Because Red has a 2.0V forward voltage while Green/Blue have ~3.2V, putting a single shared resistor on the cathode will cause Red to steal all the current, extinguishing the other colors!
3. **Respect Total Package Heat**: Running all three channels at 100% brightness (White) draws ~45 mA total, well within Uno limits when equipped with proper resistors.

steps.title: Final Review & Competencies
steps.markdownContent:
Magnificent job! In Lesson 07, you unlocked full optical color synthesis:

- You mastered additive optical color mixing (combining Red, Green, and Blue light).
- You distinguished Common Cathode (Active-HIGH, shared GND) from Common Anode (Active-LOW, shared 5V).
- You understood high-speed 490Hz/980Hz PWM duty cycles and average voltage simulation.
- You located Uno hardware PWM pins marked with `~` (3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 11) and their timers.
- You wrote modular helper functions (`setColor()`) with 8-bit `analogWrite()` (0–255).
